{
  "analyses": [
    {
      "paper_id": "doi-10-1017-s1351324909005051",
      "title": "Formal and functional assessment of the pyramid method for summary content evaluation",
      "research_question": "Can the Pyramid Method provide reliable, annotator-consistent and statistically discriminative evaluation of summary content across different summarization evaluation settings?",
      "methodology": "The paper performs a formal reliability assessment using DUC 2003 data and a functional assessment using DUC 2003, 2005 and 2006 evaluations. It measures inter-annotator agreement for Summary Content Unit and peer-summary annotation, compares independently produced Pyramid scores using ANOVA and correlations, and compares resulting system rankings. It then analyzes robustness across evaluation settings with ANOVA, Tukey HSD tests and statistical power analyses while document-set size, summary length, number of reference summaries and participating systems vary.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "Peer-summary annotation showed generally strong inter-annotator reliability, with mean alpha-Dice agreement of about 0.78 in the reported DUC 2003 comparison.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.1 Formal assessment"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Independent annotations produced score distributions with no significant annotator effect in the reported Set I ANOVAs, indicating that annotation differences had little effect on aggregate scores.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.1 Formal assessment"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Two independently annotated evaluations disagreed on only two of 120 pairwise system-ranking comparisons, providing strong functional evidence that system-level conclusions were robust to annotator choice.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.2 Functional assessment / 6 Discussion"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The evaluated system was a highly significant predictor of Pyramid score in all three DUC years, despite changes in task and evaluation conditions.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.2 Functional assessment"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Power analyses indicated that substantially fewer document sets than those used in the evaluations could still distinguish systems at the specified high-power setting.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.2 Functional assessment"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The evidence for robustness across years is partly observational rather than fully controlled because systems, procedures, tools and several task parameters changed simultaneously.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.2 Functional assessment / 8 Conclusion"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "Large-scale Pyramid evaluation is labor-intensive because important annotation stages are manual.",
        "The cross-year functional comparison is only partly controlled because multiple evaluation conditions, systems and procedures changed between DUC years.",
        "Annotator expertise and motivation may contribute to the high reliability observed in DUC 2005 and 2006, where many annotators were summarization-system developers or were supervised by the author.",
        "Reliability varied for some individual peer annotations, including reported outliers.",
        "The Pyramid representation identifies and weights shared content but does not itself provide an explanatory semantic model of relations among content units and source documents.",
        "The paper does not report an end-to-end automatic method for constructing the Pyramid content model."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": false,
        "dataset_available": false,
        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "annotation_reliability": 0.98,
        "ranking_robustness": 0.99,
        "cross_year_discrimination": 0.96,
        "statistical_power": 0.95,
        "generalization_beyond_DUC": 0.75
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "The Pyramid Method decomposes summary-content evaluation into constructing weighted shared content units and matching a candidate summary against those units.",
        "Different annotators generally produced highly similar peer annotations.",
        "Differences between annotators had little effect on average Pyramid scores in the controlled DUC 2003 comparisons.",
        "Independent Pyramid and peer annotations produced nearly identical conclusions about which systems differed significantly.",
        "System identity predicted Pyramid scores significantly in each of the three DUC years examined.",
        "The method retained useful discriminative power despite changes in document-cluster size, summary length and number of reference summaries.",
        "Manual annotation cost is a major obstacle to large-scale use.",
        "The reported reliability may partly depend on annotator expertise, supervision and motivation.",
        "The Pyramid representation measures content-selection agreement but does not explain semantic relations among the represented content units."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220597319_Formal_and_functional_assessment_of_the_pyramid_method_for_summary_content_evaluation",
      "access": "full_text"
    },
    {
      "paper_id": "2606.00093",
      "title": "Agreement Measurement for Rubric-based LLM Judges: What to Report and Why",
      "research_question": "What measurement protocol and reporting practices are necessary for human-LLM judge agreement numbers to be interpretable, reconstructible and comparable, especially when evaluations include abstentions, multiple criteria and different aggregation choices?",
      "methodology": "The paper develops a measurement-protocol view of LLM-judge evaluation by assembling established statistical results from psychometrics, econometrics and annotation research and deriving their implications for rubric-based evaluation. It proves or restates identities among binary agreement statistics, analyzes Cohen's kappa under marginal mismatch, develops abstention-handling and identification bounds, and examines multi-judge aggregation. The authors then reconstruct or reanalyze three published LLM-judge evaluations and conduct a descriptive, explicitly non-systematic coding of 24 recent LLM-as-judge papers before synthesizing the results into a reporting checklist.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "For non-degenerate binary verdict vectors, Pearson correlation, Spearman correlation, Kendall tau-b, phi and Matthews correlation are mathematically identical, so reporting several of them adds no independent evidence.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "4.1 Five Metrics, One Statistic"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Cohen's kappa differs from phi through a marginal-mismatch factor and equals phi when the human and judge positive-label rates match.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "4.2 Marginal Normalization: Kappa Versus Phi"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Excluding, recoding or retaining abstentions changes the estimand, and therefore agreement numbers produced under different abstention rules cannot be treated as measurements of the same quantity.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.1 Abstention Handling Modes"
        },
        {
          "finding": "When abstained cases are excluded, covered accuracy and coverage identify full-set forced-choice accuracy only within an interval whose width equals the uncovered fraction.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.2 Coverage and Bounds on Full-Set Accuracy"
        },
        {
          "finding": "In a reconstructed abstaining judge cascade, the same released predictions yield substantially different headline accuracies depending on abstention handling, including approximately 0.874 covered accuracy, approximately 0.73 after recoding and 0.534 with abstention retained as a third class.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.4 Example: Handling Rules and Bounds"
        },
        {
          "finding": "On the analyzed rubric benchmark, protocol choices moved reported accuracy across a range of 34.8 percentage points without changing the underlying judge verdicts.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.5 A Rubric Benchmark with Human Abstention"
        },
        {
          "finding": "A reconstructible agreement claim should report the judgment scale, target metric, contingency tables and marginals, handling of abstentions or invalid outputs, coverage, aggregation rules and ensemble conventions rather than only a headline agreement number.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "7 A Reporting Checklist"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "The literature scan of 24 papers is descriptive and non-exhaustive rather than a systematic review.",
        "The literature coding was performed by one author without independent double coding, adjudication or an inter-coder reliability statistic.",
        "The exact equivalence among the five association metrics applies only to non-degenerate binary verdicts.",
        "The asymptotic variance equivalence discussed for kappa and phi is specific to matched positive-label rates.",
        "The empirical abstention case studies are unilateral: one has judge-side abstention and another human-side abstention, rather than both sides abstaining.",
        "The rubric case study evaluates one judge model in one domain and has weak underlying judge-human agreement, limiting conclusions about how protocol effects behave for strong judges.",
        "The framework validates judges against a human reference but does not itself establish the reliability or construct validity of that human reference."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": true,
        "dataset_available": true,
        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "binary_metric_identity": 0.99,
        "kappa_marginal_effect": 0.99,
        "abstention_changes_estimand": 0.99,
        "coverage_identification_bound": 0.99,
        "protocol_effect_empirical": 0.98,
        "reporting_checklist": 0.97
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "An agreement number is meaningful only relative to the measurement protocol that defines its target population, scale and handling rules.",
        "Five commonly reported association coefficients collapse to the same statistic on non-degenerate binary verdicts.",
        "A low kappa can partly reflect different human and judge label prevalences rather than simply poor item-wise association.",
        "A confusion matrix contains diagnostic information that cannot be reconstructed from headline agreement metrics alone.",
        "Abstention should not automatically be treated as an ordinary negative verdict.",
        "Excluding abstentions changes the evaluated population to the subset on which neither side abstains.",
        "Covered accuracy cannot by itself establish performance over the full evaluation population.",
        "Identification uncertainty from unobserved abstained cases is distinct from sampling uncertainty.",
        "Undefined metrics on degenerate criteria should be reported as unavailable rather than entered as zero.",
        "Agreement among members of a judge ensemble cannot replace validation against an external human reference.",
        "Protocol choices alone can materially change reported judge performance while leaving every raw verdict unchanged.",
        "The authors provide ancillary Python scripts intended to reproduce all computed values and the literature-scan coding."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://arxiv.org/html/2606.00093",
      "access": "full_text"
    },
    {
      "paper_id": "2605.16354",
      "title": "Augmenting Human Evaluation with LLM Judges: How Many Human Reviews Do You Need?",
      "research_question": "How can LLM-generated ratings be used as auxiliary measurements to reduce human evaluation cost while retaining a principled target level of statistical precision or power?",
      "methodology": "The paper reformulates LLM-assisted evaluation as a two-stage sampling problem in which LLM ratings are collected for the full sample and human ratings for a designed subsample. It applies a doubly robust estimator whose human-rating observation probabilities are known by design, derives its asymptotic variance, and uses that variance to obtain human and LLM sample-size relationships for a target effective sample size. It then analytically studies uniform and stratified sampling designs under different assumed LLM-human predictive R-squared values and illustrates their human-review requirements.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "Because human-review probabilities are controlled and known by design, the doubly robust estimator can retain valid inference for the human-rating target even when the model predicting human ratings from auxiliary measurements is misspecified.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "2.2 The estimator"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The number of required human reviews decreases as the predictive relationship between LLM and human ratings becomes stronger and as the available LLM-rated pool becomes larger.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "3.1 Sample Size Calculations"
        },
        {
          "finding": "For a fixed predictive quality, increasing the number of LLM evaluations has diminishing returns, and the required human sample approaches a nonzero floor proportional to one minus the squared predictive correlation.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "3.1 Behavior of sample size"
        },
        {
          "finding": "If LLM ratings contain no predictive information about human ratings, increasing the LLM-rated sample does not reduce the required human-review count.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "3.1 Sample Size Calculations"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Stratifying human review according to heterogeneous LLM reliability can save human annotations by allocating more review to strata where LLM predictions are less reliable.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "3.2 Stratified sampling"
        },
        {
          "finding": "In the paper's modeled two-stratum scenarios, stratification reduced human-review requirements by up to 12.9 percent relative to uniform allocation when predictive quality differed sharply between strata.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "3.2 Comparison of designs"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The framework's numerical results are analytic design examples rather than empirical validation on a newly collected LLM-evaluation dataset.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "3 Main Results / 4 Limitations"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "The sample-size calculation requires an estimate of predictive R-squared from pilot data.",
        "Overestimating predictive R-squared because of small pilots, overfitting or distribution mismatch can cause underallocation of human review and invalidate the intended precision target.",
        "The framework treats human ratings as the target or gold standard and does not solve unreliable, inconsistent or construct-ambiguous human judgment.",
        "The main formulation covers one human rater rather than multiple-rater reliability.",
        "The examples primarily concern discrete, single-turn evaluations and require extension for multi-turn dialogue or sequential interactions.",
        "The paper provides analytic and simulated design illustrations rather than a broad empirical comparison across deployed LLM judges and real evaluation datasets."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": false,
        "dataset_available": false,
        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "doubly_robust_design_validity": 0.96,
        "human_sample_depends_on_predictability": 0.99,
        "diminishing_returns": 0.99,
        "stratified_allocation": 0.97,
        "empirical_generalization": 0.72
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "The paper treats human judgment as the inferential target and LLM judgment as auxiliary information rather than as a replacement.",
        "Human labels are observed on a designed subsample while LLM ratings can be observed for the full evaluation pool.",
        "Known sampling probabilities make the missing-human-label mechanism controlled by the investigator.",
        "A doubly robust estimator combines observed human labels with predictions derived from auxiliary information.",
        "Better prediction of human ratings reduces the amount of human review needed for a fixed precision target.",
        "LLM ratings that have zero predictive value do not reduce the necessary human sample.",
        "Adding more LLM-rated examples yields progressively smaller reductions in human annotation requirements.",
        "Human-review effort can be concentrated in strata where LLM ratings predict human ratings poorly.",
        "The required sample calculation is sensitive to the quality of the pilot estimate of predictive performance.",
        "The framework does not establish that human raters themselves are reliable.",
        "Extension to multiple human raters and multi-turn evaluations is left for future work."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://arxiv.org/html/2605.16354",
      "access": "full_text"
    },
    {
      "paper_id": "2111.09525",
      "title": "SummaC: Re-Visiting NLI-based Models for Inconsistency Detection in Summarization",
      "research_question": "Can natural-language-inference models reliably detect factual inconsistency in summaries if the granularity mismatch between sentence-level NLI training and document-level summarization evaluation is explicitly addressed?",
      "methodology": "The authors split source documents and summaries into smaller text blocks and run an NLI model over every source-summary block pair to form an NLI pair matrix. SummaC-ZS aggregates maximum entailment evidence per summary sentence without training, while SummaC-Conv bins the score distributions and learns a small convolutional aggregation layer on a subset of synthetic FactCC training data. Evaluation uses the SummaC Benchmark, which standardizes six existing factual-consistency datasets into binary classification tasks, with balanced accuracy as the primary metric, ROC-AUC as a secondary metric, and bootstrap significance tests against prior systems.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "Using sentence-level or similarly fine-grained NLI comparisons substantially improves inconsistency detection compared with applying NLI directly to full documents and summaries.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.3.3 Choice of Granularity"
        },
        {
          "finding": "SummaC-Conv achieved 74.4 percent average balanced accuracy on the six-dataset SummaC Benchmark, approximately five absolute points above the strongest reported non-NLI baseline.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.2 SummaC Benchmark Results"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Overall improvements of both SummaC variants over prior work were statistically significant under the paper's bootstrap testing procedure, with the stronger significance level reported for SummaC-Conv.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.2.1 Statistical Testing"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Using the full distribution of sentence-level entailment scores in SummaC-Conv is more robust than relying only on each summary sentence's single maximum entailment score.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.2 SummaC Benchmark Results"
        },
        {
          "finding": "NLI architecture and training data materially affect factual-consistency performance, with Transformer-based models and domain-relevant NLI data outperforming the older decomposable-attention setup used in earlier negative results.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.3.1 Choice of NLI Model"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The benchmark standardization exposes substantial variation in annotation regimes, class balance and source summarization datasets, rather than assuming that all factuality datasets measure an identical distribution.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "4 SummaC Benchmark"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "All six benchmark datasets are from news summarization, so performance outside that domain was not established.",
        "Benchmark datasets differ in annotation quality, annotator expertise, labeling schemes and class balance.",
        "Some datasets lacked existing validation/test splits, requiring the authors to construct deterministic splits.",
        "Some benchmark datasets have only one annotator per example, preventing inter-annotator reliability estimates for those datasets.",
        "Sentence-level decomposition can miss evidence requiring cross-sentence or multi-hop reasoning.",
        "The system detects inconsistency but does not itself solve factual correction or guarantee factual summaries.",
        "Performance remains far below perfect consistency detection despite outperforming the compared baselines."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": true,
        "dataset_available": true,
        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "granularity_effect": 0.99,
        "summac_conv_performance": 0.99,
        "statistical_improvement": 0.97,
        "nli_training_choice": 0.98,
        "cross_domain_generalization": 0.7
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "Earlier NLI-based factuality approaches suffered from a mismatch between sentence-level NLI training and document-level summarization inputs.",
        "SummaC represents support using pairwise NLI scores between source and summary text blocks.",
        "SummaC-ZS uses the strongest source-sentence support for each summary sentence and then aggregates across the summary.",
        "SummaC-Conv learns from the distribution of NLI scores rather than depending only on extrema.",
        "The SummaC Benchmark combines six factual-consistency datasets into a common binary classification setup.",
        "Balanced accuracy is used because the component datasets have strongly different class distributions.",
        "SummaC-Conv obtained the highest overall balanced accuracy among the compared methods.",
        "Fine textual granularity generally outperformed full-document NLI evaluation.",
        "The source and quality of NLI training data materially affected downstream consistency detection.",
        "The authors publicly released the SummaC models and standardized benchmark data.",
        "The benchmark is concentrated on news and does not establish performance in other document domains."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://arxiv.org/html/2111.09525",
      "access": "full_text"
    },
    {
      "paper_id": "2305.14627",
      "title": "Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations",
      "research_question": "How can retrieval-augmented language models generate useful long-form answers with citations, and how can citation completeness and correctness be evaluated automatically and against human judgments?",
      "methodology": "The paper introduces ALCE, an evaluation framework over 1,000 selected examples each from ASQA, QAMPARI and ELI5, paired with Wikipedia or Sphere retrieval corpora segmented into passages. Systems retrieve evidence with off-the-shelf retrievers and use several prompting or post-processing strategies to make LLMs synthesize answers and attach citations. Evaluation separately measures fluency, task-specific answer correctness, citation recall for whether claims are supported, and citation precision for whether individual citations are relevant, with NLI used for automated citation-support judgments. The authors compare multiple LLMs and retrieval strategies, perform ablations and repeated runs, and validate automatic citation metrics through human evaluation.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "Separating answer correctness from citation recall and citation precision exposes systems that produce plausible or correct text without adequate evidence attribution.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "3 Automatic Evaluation"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Current tested systems leave substantial portions of generated content unsupported by their citations; on ELI5, even strong baselines had citation recall around one half rather than complete support.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.1 Main Results"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Simple retrieval followed by placing the retrieved passages directly in the LLM context was competitive with more elaborate interaction strategies.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.1 Main Results"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Reranking multiple generated answers using automated citation recall consistently improved citation quality in the tested ASQA and ELI5 settings.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.1 Main Results"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Retrieval quality strongly constrains answer correctness and citation quality, but even oracle-like access to relevant evidence does not guarantee that an LLM will successfully use that evidence.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.3 Retrieval Analysis"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Supplying more retrieved passages did not proportionally improve performance for the tested models, indicating limitations in multi-document synthesis and susceptibility to irrelevant context.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.3 Retrieval Analysis"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Automated ALCE citation judgments agreed substantially with humans for citation recall and moderately for citation precision, with reported Cohen kappa values of 0.698 and 0.525 respectively.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "6 Human Evaluation"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Post-hoc citation assignment to closed-book answers can preserve answer correctness while still yielding poor attribution because correct generated statements may not align closely with retrieved passages.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.1 Main Results"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "Citation-support evaluation depends on the accuracy and granularity of the NLI model used as the automatic evaluator.",
        "The automatic citation-precision evaluator cannot represent partial support as accurately as human annotators.",
        "MAUVE fluency scores are sensitive to generation length and may be unstable.",
        "Automatically generated ELI5 reference claims may not cover every valid answer because the task is open-ended.",
        "The three datasets do not cover harder evidence-use settings such as multi-hop reasoning, mathematical reasoning or code generation.",
        "Experiments focus on prompting existing LLMs rather than training models specifically for citation generation.",
        "Limited model context windows constrain how many source passages can be presented simultaneously.",
        "Retrieval corpora and question-answer datasets do not directly model temporal freshness, source versioning or superseded evidence."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": true,
        "dataset_available": true,
        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "citation_dimensions_separate_failure_modes": 0.99,
        "incomplete_citation_support": 0.98,
        "reranking_improves_citations": 0.96,
        "retrieval_quality_matters": 0.99,
        "multi_source_synthesis_limit": 0.97,
        "automatic_human_agreement": 0.99,
        "posthoc_citation_limit": 0.96
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "ALCE evaluates generated answers along separate dimensions for fluency, correctness and citation quality.",
        "Citation recall asks whether generated statements are adequately supported by cited passages.",
        "Citation precision asks whether individual cited passages actually support the statement to which they are attached.",
        "The benchmark uses ASQA, QAMPARI and ELI5 questions with retrieved evidence from Wikipedia or Sphere.",
        "Simple insertion of retrieved passages into the prompt is a strong baseline for citation generation.",
        "Selecting among multiple candidate generations using citation recall improves evidence support in the tested settings.",
        "Retrieval recall provides an upper constraint on what evidence a retrieval-augmented generator can use.",
        "Models still fail to exploit some relevant evidence even when that evidence is present in their context.",
        "Adding more passages can introduce distraction and does not guarantee better synthesis.",
        "Closed-book generation followed by post-hoc citation matching produces weak evidence attribution.",
        "Automatic citation recall showed stronger human agreement than automatic citation precision.",
        "The authors released ALCE code and data publicly."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://arxiv.org/html/2305.14627",
      "access": "full_text"
    }
  ],
  "skipped": []
}
